initial_requirements: Public health organizations need an outbreak management system to support investigation, monitoring, analysis, and reporting during disease outbreaks, bioterrorism incidents, and other health events. Investigators should be able to collect information about cases, contacts, exposures, specimens, and interventions, connect related entities and events, and use the resulting information to identify and contain a health threat while protecting sensitive data.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What are the primary outcomes and success criteria you want this outbreak management system to achieve for public health investigators and decision-makers?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
The main outcome is that investigators can quickly see what is happening in an outbreak, connect the cases and exposures, and act early enough to interrupt transmission. For decision-makers, the system should give a reliable operational picture so they can prioritize resources, track response progress, and support defensible public health decisions.
Success, to me, would mean fewer missed links between people and events, faster investigation and reporting turnaround, and better coordination across the team. It also needs to protect sensitive information appropriately, because if people don’t trust the system, they won’t use it consistently.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Who are the main user groups and stakeholders that will use or rely on this outbreak management system, and what responsibilities or needs does each group have?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
The primary users are public health investigators, disease surveillance staff, and outbreak response coordinators, since they’re the ones entering, linking, and analyzing the case and contact information. They need fast data entry, the ability to track relationships across cases, exposures, specimens, and interventions, and a clear workflow for follow-up and status updates.
Decision-makers and supervisors rely on the system for situational awareness, trend review, and reporting, so they need summarized views, timelines, and confidence that the data is current. There are also lab and field partners who may contribute information or receive assignments, and they need a secure way to share only the information relevant to their role.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What key business rules should the system enforce for outbreak investigations—for example, how cases, contacts, exposures, specimens, and interventions should be linked or prioritized—and what notification or escalation steps should happen when a case is urgent, incomplete, or requires follow-up?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
At a high level, the system should make sure each contact, exposure, specimen, and intervention is tied to the right case or event, and it should preserve the relationship history when things are updated. If a case is marked urgent or high risk, it needs to surface immediately for the assigned team and move into a more active follow-up status so it doesn’t get lost in the queue.
If key information is missing, the system should flag the record as incomplete and keep it visible until required fields are filled in or the issue is explicitly deferred. For escalation, I’d expect alerts to go to the assigned investigator or supervisor first, and then to broader response leadership if there’s no action within the expected timeframe, but the exact timing and thresholds would need to be set by policy.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Are there any key constraints or boundary conditions we should design for—such as regulatory, operational, volume, connectivity, or emergency-response situations—that could limit how the system functions or require special handling?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
Yes, definitely. We have to design for privacy and public health data-sharing rules, since some information will be highly sensitive and access has to be tightly controlled by role and jurisdiction. Operationally, the system needs to keep working during surges, when there may be a lot of cases and contacts coming in at once, and it should still be usable if connectivity is spotty in the field or during emergency response.
We also need to support situations where data is incomplete or changing quickly, because outbreak work often starts before we have all the facts. I don’t know the exact regulatory standards or load thresholds yet, but those are definitely constraints we’d need to verify with the team.

turns.interviewer_utterance: When investigators or field staff are working with spotty or unavailable connectivity, what offline capabilities should the system support for creating, viewing, updating, and synchronizing outbreak records, and how should it handle conflicts when changes are made both offline and online?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
It should let users create and update the core records they need in the field, and at minimum view the cases or assignments already downloaded to the device. I’d also want it to queue changes locally so they can keep working without losing data, then sync automatically when connectivity comes back.
For conflicts, the system should not silently overwrite anything important. My preference would be to flag the conflict, keep both versions available for review, and let a designated user decide which update wins based on timestamps and data quality, but the exact merge rules would need to be agreed with the investigators.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Which external systems need to integrate with the outbreak management system—especially surveillance and laboratory systems—and what data should flow between them in each direction?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
The main integrations would likely be with surveillance systems, laboratory reporting systems, and possibly immunization or vital records systems if those are part of the investigation workflow. From those systems, we’d want case notifications, lab results, specimen details, and any relevant demographic or jurisdictional data to come into the outbreak system.
In the other direction, we’d probably send back investigation status, case identifiers, specimen requests, and possibly disposition or classification updates so those partner systems stay aligned. The exact list will depend on what systems each public health agency already uses, but the goal is to avoid duplicate entry and keep everyone working from the same current record.

turns.interviewer_utterance: When data comes in from multiple external systems, how should the outbreak management system determine whether two records refer to the same person, case, or specimen—for example, which identifiers or matching rules should it use, and when should it automatically link, flag for review, or create a new record?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
It should use a combination of strong identifiers and demographic matching, like national or local IDs where available, plus name, date of birth, sex, address, specimen accession numbers, and event dates. If there’s a high-confidence exact match on a stable identifier, the system can automatically link records, but if the match is partial or there are conflicts, it should flag them for human review instead of assuming they’re the same.
When the information is too weak or clearly inconsistent, it should create a new record and keep the potential duplicate visible for later reconciliation. I’d also want the matching rules to be configurable by agency, because what counts as a reliable identifier can vary a lot across jurisdictions and data sources.

turns.interviewer_utterance: To support compliance and accountability, what audit and traceability capabilities should the system provide—for example, which user actions and data changes must be logged, how detailed those logs should be, and how long investigators or administrators need to be able to retain and review them?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
We need a complete audit trail for anything that changes a record or a case decision, including creates, edits, deletes, status changes, linkage changes, approvals, and exports. It should capture who did it, when they did it, what changed, and ideally the before-and-after values so we can reconstruct the investigation history.
Those logs need to be detailed enough for compliance review and internal review of decisions, but I don’t know the exact retention period yet because that usually depends on agency policy and legal requirements. At minimum, investigators and administrators should be able to review the history long after the outbreak is active, and access to the audit trail itself should also be controlled.

slots.name: project_goals
slots.value: Enable investigators to quickly see what is happening in an outbreak, connect the cases and exposures, and act early enough to interrupt transmission; provide decision-makers with a reliable operational picture to prioritize resources, track response progress, and support defensible public health decisions; reduce missed links, speed investigation and reporting turnaround, improve team coordination, and protect sensitive information to maintain trust and consistent use.

slots.name: stakeholder_roles
slots.value: Primary users are public health investigators, disease surveillance staff, and outbreak response coordinators who enter, link, and analyze case and contact information; decision-makers and supervisors use the system for situational awareness, trend review, and reporting; lab and field partners may contribute information or receive assignments and need secure role-based sharing of relevant information.

slots.name: functional_needs
slots.value: Fast data entry; track relationships across cases, exposures, specimens, and interventions; clear workflow for follow-up and status updates; summarized views, timelines, and current-data reporting for decision-makers; secure sharing of information relevant to each user role.

slots.name: business_rules
slots.value: Each contact, exposure, specimen, and intervention must be tied to the correct case or event, and relationship history must be preserved when records are updated. Urgent or high-risk cases should be surfaced immediately for the assigned team and moved into active follow-up status. Incomplete records should be flagged and kept visible until required information is provided or explicitly deferred.

slots.name: data_entities
slots.value: Cases, contacts, exposures, specimens, interventions, relationship links between people and events, status updates, timelines, summarized reporting data, urgent/high-risk flags, incomplete record indicators, and relationship history.

slots.value: Use strong identifiers and demographic matching such as national or local IDs, name, date of birth, sex, address, specimen accession numbers, and event dates; auto-link on high-confidence exact matches, flag partial or conflicting matches for human review, create new records when information is weak or inconsistent, and make matching rules configurable by agency.

slots.name: external_partner_data_sharing_payloads
slots.value: Partner systems may send case notifications, lab results, specimen details, and relevant demographic or jurisdictional data into the outbreak system; the outbreak system may send back investigation status, case identifiers, specimen requests, and disposition or classification updates.

slots.name: duplicate_detection_and_merge_workflow
slots.value: Potential duplicate records should be visible for later reconciliation; high-confidence matches may link automatically, partial or conflicting matches should be flagged for human review, and unclear or inconsistent cases should result in a new record rather than automatic merge.
